book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
samples: The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.

Brian McDonald opposes two arts in Panem: Peeta's Aristotelian mimesis, which delights and instructs (his camouflage station skill and the 'right shade for sunlight on white fur' speech that eases the dying morphling's last moments), and the Capitol's 'perverse imitation' of tragedy in the arena and Caesar Flickerman's interviews, where the audience feels catharsis's pity and fear with none of its insight because they are complicit in inflicting the tragedy. Drawing on Phillip Rieff's notion of 'de-creation,' he links the Remake Center's freakish body modifications to the arena's cruelties as one abandonment of aesthetic and ethical limits, and uses Augustine's 'deceptive sense of omnipotence' from the Confessions plus Ernest Becker's causa-sui project to explain the Capitol's flight from any fixed identity ('You almost look like a real person'). The chapter closes with Katniss's recognition scene in Mockingjay: choosing the artist Peeta over the hunter Gale is how she survives having become a monster herself.

Anne Torkelson reads Panem through the Republic and the Laws: because mousike imitates states of soul and slowly molds character, Socrates polices music and poetry in the just city and fears innovation in musical modes, and the Capitol's own outlawing of songs quietly confirms music's power. She shows 'The Meadow Song' replacing Katniss's grief with hope and inspiring the flowers for Rue, the forbidden 'Hanging Tree' planting the Socratic question of whether an unjust life is a fate worse than death (paralleling Socrates's own unjust execution, the hemlock, and the nightlock pact Katniss, Gale, and Peeta make), and Rue's four notes mutating from an orchard work-signal into a salute of defiance when the District 11 man whistles them on the Victory Tour, at the cost of his life. Music, which Katniss dismisses as 'somewhere between hair ribbons and rainbows,' turns out to be the force that shapes her character and carries the revolution.

Jill Olthouse applies hermeneutics, crediting Gadamer as its key philosophical developer, to Panem's ideological battle of words and images: paradoxical metaphors like 'the girl on fire,' 'tribute,' and 'mockingjay' carry contestable associations, so interpreting them is a creative act through which Katniss is either defined by her enemies or defines herself. She traces Katniss's reinterpretations, from squirrel-prey to hunter after Peeta saves her, from staged 'star-crossed lovers' to a bond that becomes literal, to the berry suicide ploy that denies the Capitol its victory, and reads the hijacked Peeta's 'she's some kind of mutt' as the Capitol winning an interpretive round by stealing her metaphor. The chapter culminates in Katniss's creative reading of Snow's confession and her assassination of Coin, the moment she finally claims the mockingjay identity on her own terms as a fighter and messenger rather than a weapon used by others.

George Dunn tests Katniss's luck-saturated life against Kant's claim that the good will shines 'like a jewel' regardless of fortune, with Peeta's vow to 'die as myself' as the stronghold the Gamemakers cannot touch, and with Seneca's dictum that what Fortune has not given she cannot take away. He then runs Nagel's four kinds of moral luck through the trilogy: Haymitch's reaping-made alcoholism as constitutive luck, Rue's death sparing Katniss an impossible final choice as circumstantial luck, Peeta's rooftop words echoing unconsciously behind the flowers for Rue as causal luck, and the revolution's success as resultant luck without which Katniss would have been the destroyer of District 12 rather than its torchbearer. Framing the Gamemakers as Fortuna on her wheel, he ends with the berries: since Katniss can never untangle whether she held them out from love, defiance, or self-protection, even moral worth proves hostage to luck and to the opacity of our own motives.

Andrew Shaffer imagines Capitol patrons at Caesar's Bar & Grill cheering the Quarter Quell bloodbath and asks what makes their enjoyment possible, answering with Schopenhauer's 'devilish' verdict on Schadenfreude as the mark of a worthless heart, Kant's calling it a 'diabolical' vice, and Nietzsche's account of another's misfortune as the social equalizer that appeases envy. He argues the spectators need dehumanization, from Effie's 'savages' rhetoric and the prep team's scrubbing to the wolf mutts wearing Glimmer's eyes, to enjoy innocent children dying, and that the star-crossed-lovers story humanizes the tributes enough to force the unprecedented double-victor rule change. The chapter closes by turning the diagnosis on us: readers thrill to the arena too, the whole trilogy arguably runs on Schadenfreude, and even Snow's execution is staged as a spectacle of righteous pleasure in a villain's death.

book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
essays: Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head
Legal and Not So Legal Forms of Inception
Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End
Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word
An Old Man, Filled with Regret . .
Guilt Can be a Real Bitch
samples: The book's introduction frames Inception as the newest chapter in the dream-skepticism tradition: Plato's question about how we explain our perceptions of reality and Descartes's point that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, with the twist that Descartes never doubted our thoughts are our own while the film contests exactly that. It previews the volume's rival readings — the single-dream theory of the airline flight, Brophy's claim that the shared dreams are server-based electronic worlds like Second Life, and neuroscience suggesting we act on thoughts before we are aware of them. It also stakes out the ethics: inception as a violation of autonomy akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing, and the diagnosis that Inception is fundamentally a tale from the business world of corporations.

Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.

Brogaard argues the film's inception method is more science than fiction, starting from the neuroscience of dreaming: against Hobson's activation-synthesis model (and Dennett's related wake-up narrative theory, both heirs to Freud's symbol-based dream interpretation), she cites evidence that dreams arise from dopamine-driven cortical motivation areas rather than the brain stem, so streamlined, plot-driven shared dreams cannot be ruled out. Savants like Tammet and Padgett show the brain can compute super-fast below awareness, which makes sense of the film's dream-time compression. She then speculates real mechanisms for the heist — LaBerge's lucid-dream masks, transcranial magnetic stimulation plus an artificial corpus callosum to tap a subject's right hemisphere — and treats Cobb's planting of 'my father doesn't want me to be him' in Fischer as achievable today by cruder means like mind control and fear conditioning.

Andersen argues Inception goes one step deeper than Descartes's dream argument: where Descartes doubted the world but kept ownership of his thoughts, the film imagines an identity-defining conviction — Fischer's sense of his father's judgment — being implanted so it never occurs to the victim to question it, which is to co-opt subjectivity itself. He reads Nolan's whole oeuvre (Following, Memento, The Prestige, Batman Begins) as variations on manipulation by misdirection, and diagnoses Cobb's inception on Mal in Limbo as the infection of her mind with Cartesian doubt, a philosophy impossible to live by. Since a totem guards against others' dreams but not self-deception, the film's answer is not universal doubt but trust: only by opening himself to Ariadne and choosing intimacy can Cobb go home and spin the top without looking.

Rennett stages Ariadne's 'who would want to be stuck in a dream for ten years?' against Nozick's experience machine: Nozick's three reasons for staying unplugged (doing rather than merely experiencing, being a determinate person, contact with a reality deeper than human construction) map onto Cobb's reasons for leaving Limbo — he wants to actually raise his children, be a good father, and love children who can love him back rather than projections. Against Nozick, the chapter enlists Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's choice: a perceived world is real, and Inception's shared dreams pass Berkeley's intersubjective test in ways private dreams cannot (Cobb apologizes to Arthur for being shot; dream acts carry waking consequences). It concludes that reality becomes what we choose to believe — Cobb's final refusal to watch the top, like the cave prisoners rejecting release, is the power of choice.

Testerman argues the film's heist is ironic because nobody in it acts from conscious will: citing Libet's readiness-potential experiments and Penfield's stimulation cases, she claims the feeling of willing is a post-hoc 'epistemic illusion,' so Fischer's inception merely dramatizes what happens all the time — Cobb's 'all experience is inception' becomes a thesis about ordinary agency, with Spinoza's dictum that freedom is ignorance of the causes of our actions as its motto. She reads the plot through this lens: Saito's unexamined hunger for power silently drives the team's 'group will,' Cobb's 'positive emotion trumps negative emotion' tactic exploits the limbic system, and cheaper tricks (Arthur's elephant, foot-in-the-door, subliminal advertising) would have worked as well. Against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly livable, since introspection can never reach the subconscious causes of behavior.

4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative
5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide
6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus
8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse
10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree
11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True
12 The Shadow Realities of Indiana Jones
13 Pride and Prudence in the Pursuit of Knowledge Indiana Jones, René Belloq, and Irina Spalko
14 Raiders of the Lost Ark and the Numinous Presence of God
15 Indiana Jones and the Leap of Faith
16 Sacred Objects and Cosmic Justice in Indiana Jones
17 On My “Colleague” Dr. Jones and his “Publications”
18 “Sharing Your Adventures Has Been an Interesting Experience” Indiana Jones and Professional Archaeology
samples: Dean Kowalski's introduction uses the iconic theme music and Ford's underplaying of heroism to argue that Indy is expressive of the human condition: he loses fights, doesn't always choose wisely, and persists for decades despite unrequited love, estrangement from his father, and repeated failures. It poses the questions the volume pursues through the films — whether Indy should take a leap of faith about the supernatural events he witnesses, why artifacts belong in a museum, and what his 'fact, not truth' lecture (and the real Dr. Tyree 'right down the hall') means.

Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.

Edwardo Pérez reconstructs the reasoning behind Indy's unargued mantra 'It belongs in a museum' via Bentham's principle of utility: museums maximize happiness because scholars and the public can study and enjoy artifacts for generations, unlike private collectors like Panama Hat. The same calculus explains his rule-breaking — he leaves the Mayapore Sankara Stone with the villagers ('It'd be another rock collecting dust' in a museum) because a flourishing village outweighs his fortune and glory, and he concedes the government's Area 51 warehouse may have been the utility-maximizing choice for the Ark after what it did to Belloq and Toht. Indy's apparent inconsistencies thus dissolve into case-by-case consequence weighing.

Robert Mentyka reads The Adventures of Young Indiana Jones through Aristotle: Kazantzákis's causality lesson in 'Travels with Father' introduces the four causes, which the chapter applies to the TV series itself, and the final cause grounds ethics — eudaimonia is the ultimate end of all action, as young Indy learns when the Mata Hari affair in 'Demons of Deception' shows that pleasure cannot deliver fulfillment. Virtue is a mean between extremes (courage between cowardice and recklessness), acquired through vigilant practice and through community, illustrated by Indy swinging between caution and recklessness with Nancy Stratemeyer and Pancho Villa, and by exemplars like Albert Schweitzer and Ernest Hemingway. The 'adventures that made the man' were really the virtues and the people that shaped him, completed when Crusade and Crystal Skull have him accept his roles as son and father.

Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.

Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.

book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
essays: The Face Shield Is a Mirror Iron Man and You
Over Four Thousand Words to Say No
The Attack of the Chinese Room
Putting One’s Mind into a Body
Can You Find Your Moral Compass
samples: Editor Mark D. White's introduction concedes that Iron Man looks like merely 'a guy in a shiny metal suit' next to tortured heroes like Batman, then argues he nonetheless inspires serious philosophical questions: whether Tony shows responsibility commensurate with his great power, whether the technology behind the armor has a downside, whether his true superpower is the suit or Stark's intelligence, and how his alcoholism and womanizing reflect on the hero. It frames the volume with stories like 'Demon in a Bottle,' 'Armor Wars,' and 'The Mask in the Iron Man,' suggesting that tragedy, not glitz, may be the defining aspect of Tony Stark's life.

Dunn argues Iron Man personifies both the modern dream of technology multiplying human powers and the medieval chivalric ideal, presenting Descartes as Stark's philosophical forerunner whose method promised to make us 'lords and masters of nature' and whose virtue of generosity offered only vague guidance for using that power. Heidegger's warning that technology treats everything, including humans, as 'standing-reserve' frames 'Extremis,' where the serum tells Tony's brain 'the body is wrong' and rebuilds him as a technological artifact, while 'Armor Wars' — stolen designs used by villains like Stane and Spymaster, ending with Tony accidentally killing the Gremlin with his jet boots — shows technology proliferating beyond its creator's control, so the jet boots hide feet of clay.

Gangle reads Stark's escape from the Ten Rings' cave and his press-conference conversion ('I have more to offer this world than just making things to blow up') through Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology.' Analyzing the armor via Aristotle's four causes (alloy, blueprints, Stark and Jarvis, the making of a hero) shows technology as a world-revealing, creative mode whose modern essence reduces nature and people to 'standing-reserve.' By becoming the armor — 'a pilot without the plane' — Stark unites technological might with individual conscience, using technology subversively to resist technology's own logic of power without accountability, an example of Heideggerian authentic existence the reader is called to imitate.

Rieder argues Iron Man is the one 'realistic' superhero: nothing about him requires a different world, only incremental nanotech advances — precision engineering, miniaturized computing, and carbon nanotubes a hundred times stronger than steel — already pursued at MIT's Institute for Soldier Nanotechnologies. He then uses Iron Man as a nanoethics case study, pitting cost-benefit analysis (with David Schmidtz's proviso that it is necessary but not sufficient for right action) against the precautionary principle exemplified by Bill Joy's call for relinquishment, asking whether an Obadiah Stane selling 'Iron Armies' to the highest bidder is a risk we may not take even if it is improbable. He leans precautionary: we may be morally required to forgo the experiment because the world's population never consented to the risk.

Robichaud asks whether Iron Man can atone for Tony Stark's wrongs, using the Iron Monger's reprogrammed-suit example to distinguish causal from moral responsibility and to argue that omissions can be causes. Tony's negligence in running Stark Industries is blameworthy because his playboy ignorance was itself negligent (as with the Mandarin's willful ignorance), and via T. M. Scanlon's account of blame the families harmed by the illegal weapons sales are the ones most warranted in blaming him. Since 'I'm sorry' is not enough for wrongs this serious and Tony never submits to punishment, the chapter concludes that even his crusade as Iron Man to 'right the wrongs' — crushing Raza's group and collecting rogue weapons — may not yet warrant forgiveness.

White defends Tony against blame for Captain America's assassination: spearheading registration in Civil War was a tragic dilemma, and Tony took the least bad option because 'if not me, who?' — telling Cap's corpse he sacrificed their friendship to save lives. Cap's death traces through Crossbones, the mind-controlled Sharon Carter, Dr. Faustus, and the Red Skull, not any direct act of Tony's; without foreseeability or wrongdoing, the chain of 'might haves' does not add up to responsibility, just as pushing someone out of a truck's path does not make you liable for the manhole they fall into. The motivation-centered lens of Kantian deontology and Aristotelian virtue ethics supports Tony (he gave up status, friends, and Cap himself), and living with tragic choices, as he does facing the Hulk, is itself heroic.

book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
samples: Editors Bacharach and Cook argue that LEGO is not really a toy but a building medium, closer to bricks and paint than to toy-aisle items, from which toys, practical artifacts, and gallery art (Sean Kenney, Nathan Sawaya, Ai Weiwei) are all made — and that this open-endedness is what makes LEGO philosophical. They frame the volume with Aristophanes' Cloud Cuckoo Land from The Birds, noting that Unikitty's rule-free kingdom in The LEGO Movie inherits the same pointed satire of social life. The introduction asks why LEGO in particular (Serious Play, Mindstorms, Friends, the Greenpeace video) invites hard questions about how we construct ourselves and our world, closing with the Danish motto 'leg godt' — play well, and philosophize well.

Willard poses the paradox of creativity: how can a toy that promises creativity come with rigid instructions and a purist fan culture that polices what counts as legitimate building? She reads The LEGO Movie as staging three rival models — the Master Builders' unfettered recombination (Plato's Ion on poetic madness and Kant's mysterious free-playing genius), Emmet's 'thinking outside the box' that yields the mocked double-decker couch, and Finn's father's meticulous vision. Following Aristotle against Plato that poetic skill is a teachable craft, plus psychology of jazz-improvisation studies, flow states, and Zhuangzi's butcher Cook Ding, she argues creativity is the joyful mastery of a process, so following instructions is the etude-stage that builds the database of moves from which free creation grows.

Shores opens with Sophie's World comparing LEGO bricks to Democritus' indivisible, endlessly recombinable atoms, and argues LEGO is a system of play and an 'object to think with' that models how ideas and worldviews are assembled, disassembled, and rebuilt. He contrasts Plato's Republic-era suspicion that children's play must be regulated with the Socratic playfulness that treats philosophy itself as serious play, and enlists Locke and Rousseau on play-based learning and Freud on the child at play as a creative writer rearranging its world. Lord Business' Kragle shows play taken too seriously becoming inert, while Caillois' ludus/paidia distinction frames the difference between themed narrative sets, free building, and the goal-directed rigidity of the LEGO video games.

Using three scenarios — describing the Eiffel Tower by shape alone, Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater welded to its site, and original-brick houses imagined on Mykonos versus Milwaukee — Fisher defends a moderate formalism about architectural aesthetics: in the pre-1976 'original LEGO world' of standardized, uniform bricks, aesthetic properties like beauty arise from the forms themselves and their hallmark features of versatility, backwards compatibility, and ease of disassembly. Contextualist and functional-beauty accounts of the anti-formalists fail for LEGO architecture because any original-brick design can be built anywhere, at any time, for any function or none, so context cannot fix the structure's aesthetic identity. He extends the point to real-world architectural models, which likewise bear no actual functional loads and are appreciated outside context.

Gettings asks whether LEGO set #21103, the Cuusoo DeLorean Time Machine, is numerically identical to Team BTTF's original fan design — and why the fans deserve credit and royalties. Neither matter (his 1982 attic spaceship with bricks replaced one by one) nor form (a license plate added here or there) settles identity, as the Ship of Theseus puzzle and Hobbes' reassembly variation show, analyzed through Aristotle's matter/form distinction for substances. He adopts the causal/historical view: the released set continuously descends from the fans' submission just as the adult author descends from the boy who built the spaceship, and this same historical origin, in Lockean fashion, is what grounds the designers' labor-mixing property right — the musician-and-producer analogy explaining why Team BTTF keeps the larger share of credit.

Robson argues that The Man Upstairs' real moral flaw is neither stinginess toward Finn nor mere instruction-following, both of which he defends, but 'rule worship': treating LEGO construction instructions — rules with at best conventional status like chess or etiquette rules — as sacrosanct commandments to be followed for their own sake. The contrast is with Kant, who does claim absolute status for central moral rules such as the prohibition on lying, and with the moral/conventional distinction from psychologists like Kelly and Stich that The Man cannot grasp. Emmet's rule-following differs because it serves goals like fitting in, and the flaw scales from office Micromanagers and Velma Staplebot to Inspector Javert and the mafioso, showing how misdirected rule worship becomes genuinely vicious.

book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
essays: Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight
Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil
Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the
The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future
The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
samples: Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction argues that videogames, and Zelda in particular, deserve philosophy because the gamer actively guides Link instead of passively watching, which raises questions about Link's will, Hyrule's space and time, the Triforce, timeline theories, and death. It surveys the franchise from the 1986 NES original through Phantom Hourglass and the fandom culture around it. Its central move is reading Plato's Meno — Socrates questioning the slave boy until the boy truly knows the doubled square — as the model of the 'AHA!' feeling, which it parallels to Link triumphantly hoisting a dungeon item like the ladder while the four rising notes play.

Jonathan Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, and feel touched when Aryll gives him her telescope, given that none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never call the police when Aryll is kidnapped), Carroll's thought theory (on-screen monsters act too fast for conscious thought), and Walton's pretend theory (we cannot voluntarily stop seeing the sail as a sail). Instead he proposes a multi-level mind — drawing on Plato's Republic (the thirsty non-drinker and Leontius and the corpses) plus Fodor's modules and Grodal's local/global appraisals — on which lower-level processes react to Hyrule as real while the global appraisal knows it is only a game.

Douglas Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warping degrades 'environmental presence' — the feeling of being in a virtual place — by privileging destination over journey, just as Wolfgang Schivelbusch said railway travel annihilated space and time for nineteenth-century passengers. Using Castells's contrast between spaces of flows and spaces of places and Michel de Certeau's opposition of the panoptic map view to embodied everyday experience, he shows how the map-grid teleport interface turns Hyrule's ocean into abstract, disposable space. He concedes warping is a defensible design compromise, but insists that goal-oriented play crowds out the sense of place that makes virtual worlds valuable as more than games.

Robert Arp and Dennis Milarker teach informal logic through Zelda, opening with Arp's own fallacious 'all gamers are geeks' hasty generalization and stereotypes about Miyamoto's Japanese heritage. They standard-form arguments about which Zelda game is chronologically first, distinguish deductive from inductive reasoning (the Best Buy Wii camp-out, expectations for The Adventure of Link's side-scrolling perspective), and run through fallacies: inappropriate authority, the Atari false dilemma (the TV was on channel 4), equivocation on release order versus story order, ad hominem, and the slippery slope against Doom and Grand Theft Auto. The lesson is that Ganon and gamers alike must give good arguments, since bad reasoning shapes laws, beliefs, and lives.

Toni Fellela gives an existentialist reading of Zelda, confessing she leaves Ocarina of Time and Twilight Princess permanently paused before the final Ganon fight because the meaning lies in the process of becoming, not the ending. Sartre's existence precedes essence structures Link's growth from a swordless Kokiri boy collecting equipment into the hero; Nietzsche's death of God ('we must become gods') fits Link restoring meaning to a godless Hyrule, while Camus's Sisyphus dignifies the repetitive drudge work of slashing grass for rupees. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy anchors the chapter's payoff: even the most mundane tasks — in a camp or a laundromat or Hyrule Field — become bearable and meaningful when connected to a future goal, which is why the author can play for four hours straight.

Anna Janssen reads Zelda as a meditation on death: Link embodies the worst version of immortality, an eternal purgatory of endless resurrection for the player's benefit, while the dungeon bosses — who stay dead once defeated — are the only truly mortal, and hence most human, beings in Hyrule. Hegel's demand that man reconcile himself with mortality, Nietzsche's erosion of dualist soul-belief, and Bernard Williams's worries about the tedium of immortality frame the discussion, with Wind Waker's reincarnating hero giving the immortal-soul view its due. Turning off the console becomes a metaphor for the unknowable nothingness of death, and the series' formula and save-games a structured coping alternative to a chaotic universe.

book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
essays: Introduction Doing Philosophy in the Wasteland
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Max's journeys across the Wasteland mirror the activity of philosophy itself — frustrating, difficult, often painful, but eventually enlightening — as the man who 'runs from the living and the dead' is drawn into savior roles he tries to evade in every film. It frames the book's guiding questions (what politics could we build, what ethics could we salvage for parts after the fall) and previews essays on the franchise's politics, heroics, ethics, and aesthetics, closing on George Miller's chord of hope.

Skoble argues the Mad Max world is misread as anarchy: Immortan Joe, Aunty Entity, and Humungus are genuine rulers, so the Wasteland depicts tyrannical bad government, not 'no rulers'. Against Hobbes's claim that only fear of a sovereign produces order, he cites organically evolved order (medieval merchant law, the common law, private arbitration firms) and Locke's mere 'inconveniences' of statelessness to argue peaceful anarchism is possible and stable. Thunderdome's 'two men enter, one man leaves' shows the films' dispute resolution is power-based trial by combat, not the consent-based voluntary order anarchism envisions.

Spanakos and Drake argue that although the films look Hobbesian — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' on roads without guardrails — rule in the Wasteland is never sustained by violence alone. Humungus needs the Toadie's epithets ('Lord Humungus... the Ayatollah of Rock and Rolla') and Immortan Joe rules through water rituals and the Valhalla myth that send War Boys kamakrazee willingly, believing they pursue their own glory. Drawing Weber's power/authority distinction, Arendt on power as people acting in concert, and above all Byung-Chul Han, they argue power takes its place 'in the soul of the other' through ritual, habit, and titles, turning into violence only when mediation fails.

Littmann treats Hobbes's Leviathan as a survival manual for post-apocalyptic Australia: the films illustrate his three causes of conflict — resource wars over guzzoline and water, preemptive strikes, and glory (the Nightrider's radio rant, Wez's stunts, the War Boys' 'Witness me!'). Bartertown's Thunderdome covenant and 'bust a deal, face the wheel' exemplify the social contract enforced by an absolute sovereign like Aunty Entity, while divided power (Master Blaster versus Aunty) courts civil war. He concludes Hobbes errs twice: Max's selfless acts (sparing Blaster, transfusing Furiosa) refute psychological egoism, and concentrating power in an Immortan Joe invites the very violence it fears — democracy removes leaders without blood.

Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.

Jones argues the franchise is neither post-apocalyptic nor dystopian: fuel keeps being produced, blood can still be typed, livestock and camel trains survive the pox-eclipse, and Max can rebuild his Interceptor, so the catastrophe was devastating but never global — Perth may be untouched. Nor is it a dystopia in the sense of Mill's coining (the opposite of More's utopia), because people demonstrably choose to live there: Bartertown boasts brothels, barbers, doctors, and a working methane plant, and Aunty Entity is a soft-hearted despot who spares Max against her own decree. A world can contain dystopian communities — the Citadel, Bartertown — without being a dystopia.

book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
essays: Part Five D Is for Destiny
None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where
Keep the Needle on the Record
samples: The editor's introduction retells her childhood memory of being left behind at a Wisconsin carnival, narrated in Lost-style 'flashback' and 'flash-sideways' segments, to argue that the show grips everyone because it stages the universal fear of being cut off from all we know and love. She calls this a philosophical fear that forces the questions 'Why am I here? Does my life matter?' and then previews the volume's five parts: time travel metaphysics (Fortune), epistemology (Origin), social and political philosophy (Unity), ethics (Necessity), and religion (Destiny).

Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.

Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.

Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.

Barnbaum treats the season 6 flash-sideways as counterfactual conditionals and evaluates them with David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics: in the closest possible world where James Ford's parents were still conned but he never became a grifter, Sawyer plausibly becomes a cop, whereas a world in which Jack fathers a child with Juliet demands too many extra changes to count as close to ours. She pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance - applied to dividing the crash survivors' water, where Jack's life-saving skill could justify unequal shares - as another famous hypothetical thought experiment whose conclusion rests on what people would agree to in the Original Position.

Taliaferro and Kastrul ask what the reader would do in the castaways' place, using Aristotle's view that character is a disposition to act under other conditions to assess Mr. Eko, Ben, Michael, Charlie, and Sawyer: people are not merely what they do but what they would do. Plato's Ring of Gyges, quoted at length, tests whether characters like Sun behave honestly only when watched. Against the idea that the island could reverse all values, they argue morality cannot be completely relative to context - invoking Chesterton's 'Thou shalt not steal' on the remotest star - and place Lost in the island-narrative tradition of the Odyssey and Robinson Crusoe as a story of the journey of the soul.

book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
essays: “It’s Like Watching a Dog Play the Piano”
“All That Is Solid Melts into Air”
Each of Us Would See Ourselves
Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel
Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle
“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”
“I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”
samples: The editors introduce the volume by framing Mad Men as a show that immerses viewers in the morally ambiguous world of 1960 Madison Avenue, where we find ourselves rooting for Don Draper to sell cigarettes, hide affairs, and conceal his stolen identity while cringing at the office's treatment of women. They argue the series teaches uncomfortable truths about the early 1960s (drinking, smoking, systemic sexism, racism, homophobia) while dramatizing how people experienced era-defining events as they happened, and so helps us understand both past and present. The chapters that follow, they say, are written by fans for fans who want to think further about the role of women, the morality of advertising, and how to lead a meaningful life.

Schurtz argues the Mad Men characters are not stupid but epistemically bounded by what their era counts as a reason: Don dismisses Dr. Guttman's 'death wish' research (and the proto-Marlboro-Man danger angle) because a research psychologist's testimony does not register as expertise for him, and the senior partners ignore Pete's correctly pro-Kennedy insight because a junior account executive's word is not a justifier. Working through knowledge as justified true belief (Betty is justified but wrong to believe her husband is Don Draper), the chapter moves from epistemic individualism to social epistemology (testimony, expert disagreement) and finally standpoint epistemology, illustrated by the Belle Jolie secretaries whose 'moron' insight Peggy vindicates with the winning pitch. The upshot: sexism, closeted gay life (Salvatore in 'The Hobo Code'), and Betty's dry-cleaning-bag ignorance persist because 1960 society does not distribute justifying testimony to women, the young, or the marginalized.

Dunn reads Mad Men through Plato's Republic: the passions are the 'mad masters' Cephalus describes, embodied in Pete Campbell's au pair indiscretion and remorse, and because passions cannot tell staged appearance from reality, the mimetic perfection of Don's 'You're a whore' scene with Betty grips viewers exactly as Plato feared televised drama would, watering the parts of the soul that should be ruled. He extends the point to advertising: Don's 'I make pictures where people appear to be in love' and 'love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' work because mimesis bypasses reason and attaches feeling to images, while Aristotle's account of imitation shows drama can also train virtue by making us delight in what we should. Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air' frames the title sequence, where Don's office dissolves past advertising images revealed as empty simulacra, until the final shot restores the convincing façade of his confidence.

Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.

Fritz applies Nietzsche's On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life and the Genealogy to the dialectic of remembering and forgetting: Pete cannot 'have done' with anything, so Ken Cosgrove's Atlantic Monthly story and Peggy's promotion become 'vermin' that eat into him, his reactive rancor and entitlement driving him to make Trudy broker his bad talking-bear story. Peggy is the opposite extreme of active forgetting, from not registering her own pregnancy to telling Pete flatly 'I had your baby and I gave it away. I wanted other things,' after Don's hospital advice that 'This never happened. It'll shock you how much this never happened.' Don knows forgetting is the strength of strong natures (the $5,000 offer to Adam, 'my life only goes in one direction, forward'), yet the Carousel's home-movie slides and other external triggers keep forcing the past back on him, so only Peggy fully inhabits the Nietzschean ideal.

Belliotti tests Roger Sterling against three existential standards. Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage fits him 'crisply': his quips about the chase, drinking 'because it's what men do,' and the penny-jar view of marriage reveal flight from commitment and terror of boredom, and even his twenty-year marriage to Mona lacked Kierkegaard's passionate inwardness, making it objectively true but existentially inauthentic. Measured by Nietzsche he falls between the last man who wants an agency 'where everybody has a summer house' and the will-to-power grand transcender he never becomes, oscillating between frustration and boredom; measured by Heidegger he settles for chatter, clings to fixity, and reflects on mortality only briefly after his heart attacks. The verdict: significantly inauthentic, capped by the blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' serenade that makes Don whisper 'Can we go?'

samples: Robert Fudge weighs whether Metallica's emotionally violent music corrupts or improves moral character. Against Plato's banishment of passion-stirring art (anger in 'Enter Sandman', indignation in '. . . And Justice for All'), he uses Aristotle's catharsis and the golden mean of healthy anger: 'One' purges pity and fear, and Hetfield's 'St. Anger' purged the rage behind his alcoholism. He then extends Adam Smith's empathy-based account - imaginative placement in the landmine victim's or addict's position - to argue the songs refine moral judgment, even making us question Kant's absolute duty against suicide by confronting the case where the body is a 'holding cell'.

William Irwin traces Hetfield's journey through three sets of virtues: rejecting the Christian virtues of his Christian Science upbringing ('The God That Failed' as Nietzschean slave morality and Marx's opium of the masses), adopting the warrior virtues of Kill 'Em All (life as Hobbesian war, Nietzsche's will to power and 'no remorse'), and finally embracing Buddhist virtues on St. Anger. The warrior code fails without stoicism and collapses into addiction and despair, while the four noble truths - suffering caused by craving ('Frantic', 'Sweet Amber') - fit Hetfield's recovery and growing compassion.

Bart Engelen reads 'Master of Puppets' and Hetfield's alcoholism as a case study in akrasia: the Socratic paradox from Plato's Protagoras, Plato's divided soul from the Republic, and Aristotle's weak-willed agent who knows the good but cannot act on it all describe the addict's 'struggle within'. Using Frankfurt's distinction between first- and second-order desires, he argues Hetfield became an 'unwilling addict' - and genuinely irrational - only when he stopped endorsing his desire to drink, and that recovery works through pre-commitment strategies like rehab, avoiding drinking cues, and relying on others.

Thomas Nys argues Metallica's early message of nonconformity and individuality ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath') converges with Mill's On Liberty: conformity withers human capacities and breeds a stagnant society. Mill's higher pleasures and Nozick's experience machine show why real happiness requires autonomy and earned achievement rather than passive pleasure - the point of 'Escape''s 'Life's for my own to live my own way'. He reads 'Leper Messiah' and 'Eye of the Beholder' as Metallica's versions of Mill's defense of free inquiry and truth against mindless conformity and censorship.

Jeremy Wisnewski claims Metallica is an existentialist band: Kill 'Em All answers Camus' absurd by creating meaning through chosen, expressive projects ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath'), Ride the Lightning's catalogue of deaths ('Fight Fire with Fire' to 'Fade to Black') individualizes us in the Heideggerian confrontation with our own death, and Master of Puppets dramatizes Sartrean bad faith - the 'Sanitarium' label, the soldier as 'Disposable Hero', the addict's lost freedom. He concludes that accusing Metallica of selling out with the Black Album is itself bad faith, since authenticity has no fixed content.

Philip Lindholm reads Metallica through Kierkegaard's demand for subjectivity: the soldier in 'One' crying 'Oh please God help me' exemplifies becoming a single individual before God against the untruth of the crowd, and 'The Struggle Within' stages Either/Or's passionate choice that decides the self. He then shows Hetfield himself living the inauthentic masked life Kierkegaard condemns - 'I was James Hetfield of Metallica' - until rehab forced the honest self-disclosure ('The God That Failed' and 'Until It Sleeps' mourning his parents) that marks a move toward authentic individuality.
